procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Government on November 18, 1968, preferring 14 charges against the petitioner under s. 46(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, and suspending him from his office under s. 46(3). Also, the direction under s. 47 to the Assistant Commissioner to take charge of the Math.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Petitioner filed a petition under Art. 226 in the High Court challenging provisions of the Act as ultra vires. This was dismissed as premature.
2. An appeal to the Letters Patent bench failed.
3. A writ petition filed by the petitioner was allowed by the High Court on November 8, 1966. This matter ultimately came up in appeal to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner approached the Supreme Court under Art. 32 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of ss. 46 and 47 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, as violative of his fundamental rights under Arts. 14, 19(1)(f), 25(1) and 26(b) and (d). He also alleged mala fide action against the respondent.

issue.issue_text: Whether the combined effect of sections 46 and 47 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, violates the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26 and 31 of the Constitution.

facts: The petitioner, the Mathadhipathi (head) of Sri Swami Hathiramji Math, was suspended from his office under section 46 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, pending an inquiry into fourteen charges against him.

Under section 47 of the same Act, the Assistant Commissioner of the Endowments Department was appointed to manage the day-to-day administration of the Math and its properties temporarily during the inquiry.
The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of these sections, arguing they violated his fundamental rights, particularly those under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution.
law: Article 25(1) guarantees the fundamental right to freely profess, practice, and propagate religion.
Article 26(b) grants a religious denomination complete autonomy in deciding its essential rites and ceremonies, free from outside interference.
Article 26(d) gives a religious denomination the fundamental right to administer its property in accordance with the law.
application: Regarding Article 25(1), the Court found that the petitioner had not been prohibited or debarred from professing, practicing, or propagating his religion. He was still able to enter the Math and exercise this right.

Regarding Article 26(b), the Court determined that nothing in sections 46 or 47 empowered the Commissioner or the appointed administrator to interfere with the Math's autonomy in religious matters, such as deciding on essential rites and ceremonies. Furthermore, no evidence was presented to show that any such interference had actually occurred.

Regarding Article 26(d), the Court reasoned that the provisions of section 47 did not permanently take away the right of administration from the religious denomination. The appointment of an administrator was a temporary measure, effective only while the Mathadhipathi was suspended. The Court distinguished this from a permanent vesting of control in an outside authority, which would be unconstitutional. The arrangement was a temporary solution to a vacancy, not a complete removal of the denomination's right to administer its property.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the combined effect of sections 46 and 47 of the Act did not violate the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution. The provisions were deemed to be temporary administrative arrangements that did not infringe upon the petitioner's right to practice religion or the religious denomination's autonomy in religious matters and its right to administer its property. Therefore, the petitioner's challenge was rejected.

issue.issue_text: Whether the exercise of power by the Commissioner under section 47 of the Act prohibits or debars the petitioner from professing, practicing, and propagating his religion, thereby violating Article 25(1) of the Constitution.

facts: The petitioner, a Mathadhipathi (head of a Math), was suspended from his office under section 46 of the Act.
Following the suspension, the Commissioner, exercising powers under section 47, appointed an Assistant Commissioner to manage the day-to-day administration of the Math.
The petitioner claimed that this action, particularly the appointment of an administrator, debarred him from practicing and propagating his religion.
law: Article 25(1) of the Constitution guarantees the fundamental right to freely profess, practice, and propagate religion.
application: The Court found that the petitioner had not provided any evidence to establish that he was actually prohibited or debarred from professing, practicing, and propagating his religion.
The Court noted that even if the Math was guarded by police, this did not mean the petitioner was prevented from entering the premises to exercise his fundamental religious rights.
The Court characterized the Commissioner's action under section 47 as a temporary administrative arrangement to manage the Math's affairs during the petitioner's suspension.
This administrative action was seen as distinct from and not interfering with the petitioner's personal right to practice his religion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the exercise of power by the Commissioner under section 47 did not violate the petitioner's fundamental right under Article 25(1), as the petitioner had not been prohibited or debarred from professing, practicing, and propagating his religion. The Court, therefore, rejected this challenge.

issue.issue_text: Whether sections 46 and 47 of the Act empower the Commissioner to interfere with the autonomy of a religious denomination in deciding essential rites and ceremonies, in contravention of Article 26(b) of the Constitution.

facts: The petitioner, a Mathadhipathi, was suspended from his office under section 46(3) of the Act pending an inquiry.
Under section 47, an Assistant Commissioner was appointed to manage the day-to-day administration of the Math and its endowments.

The petitioner argued that this appointment interfered with the complete autonomy of the religious denomination in matters of essential rites and ceremonies, thus violating Article 26(b) of the Constitution.
law: Under Article 26(b) of the Constitution, a religious denomination enjoys complete autonomy in deciding what rites and ceremonies are essential according to its religious tenets.
No outside authority has the jurisdiction to interfere with the denomination's decisions in such matters.
application: The Court examined the text of sections 46 and 47 of the Act.
It found that there is nothing in the language of these sections that empowers the Commissioner to interfere with the religious denomination's autonomy in deciding essential rites and ceremonies.
The Court also noted that it had not been shown that the Commissioner, or the Assistant Commissioner put in charge of day-to-day affairs, had actually interfered in such matters.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court rejected the argument, concluding that since sections 46 and 47 do not grant the Commissioner the power to interfere with essential religious rites and ceremonies, and no such interference was proven to have occurred, there was no contravention of Article 26(b).

issue.issue_text: Whether the provisions of section 47 of the Act, which allow for the temporary appointment of an administrator, take away the fundamental right of a religious denomination to administer its property according to law, as guaranteed by Article 26(d) of the Constitution.

facts: Under section 47 of the Act, an Assistant Commissioner was temporarily appointed to manage the day-to-day administration of a Math.

This appointment was made because the head of the Math (the mathadhipathi) was suspended pending an inquiry into serious charges against him, including misappropriation of funds and leading an immoral life.
law: Article 26(d) of the Constitution guarantees a religious denomination the fundamental right to administer its property 'according to law'.
A law that takes away the right of administration from the hands of a religious denomination 'altogether' and vests it 'for all time' in another authority would violate Article 26(d).
application: The Court determined that section 47 does not take away the right of administration 'altogether' or permanently. It only provides for a temporary arrangement in specific situations, such as when the head of the Math is suspended pending an inquiry.

The Court contrasted section 47 with a previous, unconstitutional law (s. 56 of a repealed Act) which had allowed the Commissioner to deprive a Mahant of his administrative rights at any time, even without any negligence or maladministration. Section 47, in contrast, clearly defines the limited conditions under which an administrator can be appointed.
The appointment of an administrator in this case was not arbitrary but was a direct result of a pending inquiry into serious charges against the petitioner.

Therefore, the power exercised under section 47 is a temporary measure applied under specific, legally defined circumstances and does not permanently divest the religious denomination of its right to administer its property.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, holding that section 47 of the Act does not violate the fundamental right under Article 26(d). The provision for a temporary administrator is a legally justified measure for specific situations and does not take away the religious denomination's right of administration altogether.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the combined effect of sections 46 and 47 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, violates the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26 and 31 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The combined effect of sections 46 (which allows for an inquiry into charges against a Mahant) and 47 (which allows for suspension pending inquiry) is unconstitutional as it violates Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26, and 31.
The action taken by the respondent (the State) against the petitioner, including framing charges and ordering suspension, was a case of mala fide action.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments are not detailed in the provided text, but they would have defended the constitutionality of sections 46 and 47 of the Act as valid regulatory measures.
The respondent gave an undertaking that the inquiry being conducted under section 46 would be concluded within three months, suggesting the measures were temporary and procedural.

The respondent agreed to keep accounts of the amounts spent on feeding sadhus and on the management of the math property, implying their actions were aimed at proper administration and accountability.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the exercise of power by the Commissioner under section 47 of the Act prohibits or debars the petitioner from professing, practicing, and propagating his religion, thereby violating Article 25(1) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner's suspension from Mahantship under section 47, as part of the broader constitutional challenge, interferes with his right to profess, practice, and propagate his religion as guaranteed by Article 25(1).
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments are not explicitly stated in the text. However, their position, accepted by the court, would be that the temporary suspension and appointment of an administrator relate to the secular, administrative functions of the Mahant and do not interfere with the petitioner's personal religious rights under Article 25(1).

arguments.issue_text: Whether sections 46 and 47 of the Act empower the Commissioner to interfere with the autonomy of a religious denomination in deciding essential rites and ceremonies, in contravention of Article 26(b) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The inquiry under section 46 and suspension under section 47 constitute an interference with the autonomy of the Math, a religious denomination, in managing its own affairs in matters of religion, which is protected by Article 26(b).
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments are not detailed in the text. The implied argument, which the court accepted, is that the state's actions under sections 46 and 47 pertain to the secular administration and the conduct of the trustee, not the 'essential rites and ceremonies' or core religious affairs of the denomination.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the provisions of section 47 of the Act, which allow for the temporary appointment of an administrator, take away the fundamental right of a religious denomination to administer its property according to law, as guaranteed by Article 26(d) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The appointment of an Assistant Commissioner to manage the Math's affairs and endowments, even temporarily, violates the denomination's right to administer its own property under Article 26(d).
The petitioner pressed for the right to continue taking the 'padakanukas' (personal offerings), asserting his role in the financial administration of the Math.
respondent_arguments: The appointment of an administrator is a temporary measure for day-to-day administration pending an inquiry into mismanagement, which is a valid regulatory step to protect the endowment's property.

The respondent agreed to the petitioner taking the 'padakanukas' provided he kept an account, and also agreed to keep accounts of all expenditures, demonstrating that the intervention was for accountability and not to expropriate the Math's property.

cases.principle: A law that takes away the right of administration from a religious denomination and vests it in another authority violates the right guaranteed under Art. 26(d) of the Constitution. It was also relied on for the principles that freedom of religion extends to religious practices and that a Mahant is entitled to the protection of Art. 19(1)(f).

cases.case_name: H. H. Sudhundra Thirtha Swamiar v. Commissioner for Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments, Mysore
cases.principle: A statutory provision allowing for a suit to be filed in a court to remove a trustee of a math for specified reasons (similar to those in s. 46 of the Act) was constitutionally valid.

The government had no jurisdiction to suspend a Mahant when it virtually amounted to a removal, which could only be done in the manner specifically provided by the statute (s. 52 of the repealed Act).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A law which allows for the appointment of an administrator over the property of a religious denomination does not violate the right to administer property under Article 26(d) of the Constitution, provided that the law does not take away the right of administration from the religious denomination altogether and vest it permanently in another authority. Such a law is also not in contravention of Article 26(b) if it does not empower interference with the autonomy of the religious denomination in deciding essential religious rites and ceremonies, nor does it violate Article 25(1) if it does not prohibit or debar a person from professing, practicing, and propagating their religion.
obiter: A law that allows a commissioner to deprive a religious head of the right to administer trust property at any moment, even without negligence or maladministration, would be an unconstitutional restriction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that sections 46 and 47 of the Act are constitutionally valid as they impose reasonable restrictions in the public interest on the secular and temporal duties of a Mahant as a trustee. The power to inquire into charges of misconduct and suspend the Mahant pending that inquiry is a necessary and reasonable procedural safeguard to protect the institution's property and ensure the integrity of the investigation. These actions do not constitute a complete takeover of the religious denomination's right to administration, nor do they interfere with core religious affairs, as they are conditional, temporary, and subject to quasi-judicial proceedings and judicial review.
legal_tests_applied: The 'reasonable restrictions in the interest of the general public' test under Article 19(1)(f) to determine if limitations on the Mahant's property rights are valid.
The distinction between the secular/temporal administration of a religious institution and its core 'matters of religion' to analyze claims under Articles 25 and 26(b).
The test for a violation of Article 26(d), which asks whether a law 'takes away the right of administration from the hands of a religious denomination altogether and vests it in any other authority'.
why_appellant_lost: The court held that the state's power to inquire into and suspend a Mahant for misconduct, such as breach of trust, mismanagement, or leading an immoral life, pertains to the secular and temporal aspects of his role as a trustee, not his core religious functions protected by Articles 25 and 26(b).

The suspension pending inquiry was deemed a 'necessary and reasonable part of the procedure' to prevent the Mahant from tampering with evidence, thus satisfying the 'reasonable restrictions' test under Article 19(1)(f).

The temporary appointment of an administrator under section 47 was distinguished from a complete and permanent takeover of the Math's administration, which would violate Article 26(d). The court found it to be a conditional and temporary measure, not an absolute vesting of control in another authority.

The challenge under Article 14 failed because the Act provides for quasi-judicial proceedings before the Commissioner and the right to challenge any removal order in a court of law, with a further right of appeal, ensuring the process is not arbitrary.
why_respondent_won: The state successfully established that the impugned sections are valid regulatory measures aimed at ensuring the proper administration of a public religious institution's property and the fitness of its head.

The restrictions were found to be reasonable and in the public interest because they address situations like a Mahant's unsound mind, breach of trust, or immoral life, which are detrimental to the institution he heads.
The power of suspension was successfully defended as an essential procedural tool to ensure the integrity of the inquiry into serious charges against the Mahant.

The statutory scheme was shown to contain sufficient procedural safeguards, including quasi-judicial proceedings and the right to judicial review, which negated the appellant's claims of arbitrariness and unconstitutionality.
policy_considerations: There is a significant public interest in ensuring that a mathadhipathi, who is in charge of a public institution and its properties, can be removed if he is unfit to perform his duties due to unsound mind, physical infirmity, breach of trust, or leading an immoral life.

The integrity of an inquiry into misconduct requires procedural safeguards, and the power to suspend the person being investigated is a necessary measure to prevent them from tampering with evidence and defeating the purpose of the inquiry.

While a religious denomination has the right to administer its property, this right is not absolute and can be reasonably restricted by law to prevent mismanagement and protect the endowment for the benefit of the public and the institution's followers.
